# Abstract: 
Give a title to your project. In an abstract of 200 words or less, describe what is
the main question you aim to answer, and a brief summary of your current results.

- TITLE: Investigating Possible Income-Dependence in Disease and Illness
- This is an observational study using two publicly available data sets to analyze correlation between income and various health statuses. We investigate using median household income by county in the United States data from the US Census Bureau and population health data by county in the United States by the CDC. Using the computational tool R, we combine the data sets and isolate comparisons for analysis with the following findings. Health status seems to be negatively correlated with income. That is, the data shows counties with higher median household incomes had less adverse health statuses across various types of health status and various income brackets. The report will delve into the method and matter of this study and provide visual maps which depict the correlation we found.

# Intro
What is the central question that motivates your analysis? Who may this analysis
benefit? Are you trying to train a model, test a hypothesis, classify objects apart? Why? This has to
be written with proper grammar and syntax: sentences, paragraphs, and a narrative structure.

- The question we are seeking to answer is whether income has an effect on disease. Will median household income show a correlation to disease proclivity? This information would be beneficial in creating policy to target decreasing disease in populations who are affected more and prevention in populations who aren't. Alternatively, certain companies and investors may be able to benefit from such a relationship being found by allowing insight into the likelihood of certain investments succeeding in a population due to their proximity to disease and their relative wealth.

To realize these possible benefits, we are creating correlation maps using publicly available data on the incomes of household in the US and comparing these numbers to CDC estimates from 2025 for health status.

# Data
What is the data available for performing the analysis? Where did you retrieve these data from? What are the variables and number of observations available? What steps where performed to clean the data? If the data is obtained via randomized simulations, clarify the data generating procedure

- US Census Bureau's data set for "Median Household Income in the Past 12 Months in 2023"
@ https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT5Y2023.B19013
This data set includes 3222 observations across 5 variables representing the geographic ID of a county, the name of the county, the median income, the margin of error, and the FIPS codes of the households surveyed. We renamed the variables and removed unneeded columns for clarity and used the FIPS codes in the 6th column against the next data set.
```{r}
mhi <- read.csv("ACSDT5Y2023.B19013-Data.csv") 
## median household income by county data
names(mhi)[c(2, 3)] <- c("County Name", "Income (USD)")
mhi <- mhi[, -c(4, 5)]

head(mhi)
```
- CDC data set for "Local Data for Better Health, County Data in 2025"
@ https://data.cdc.gov/500-Cities-Places/PLACES-Local-Data-for-Better-Health-County-Data-20/swc5-untb/about_data
This data set includes 229298 observations across 22 variables representing both location names (geographic ID, state name, etc) and the estimates for measures (health outcomes, health status, disability, etc) within those locations. We found the FIPS codes for each observation's location to compare data sets. We renamed the variables and removed unneeded columns for clarity and used the FIPS codes in the last column against the previous data set to construct our correlation maps.
```{r}
dp <- read.csv("PLACES__Local_Data_for_Better_Health,_County_Data,_2025_release_20261102.csv")
## disease percentage by county data
names(dp)[c(4, 10, 21)] <- c("County Name", "Percentage of Population", "Health Status")
dp <- dp[, -c(1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 18, 19, 20)]

head(dp)
```
- Combining the data sets
```{r}
mhi$FIPS = substr(mhi$GEO_ID, nchar(mhi$GEO_ID) - 4 ,nchar(mhi$GEO_ID))
dp$FIPS = as.numeric(dp$LocationID)
#clean each dataset and have a similar row of FIP codes
comp_data = merge(mhi, dp, by = "FIPS", check.names = FALSE)
#combine the two datasets into a single dataset to make comparisons easier

comp_data = comp_data %>% select(
  FIPS,
  `County Name.x`,
  `County Name.y`,
  `Income (USD)`,
  `Health Status`,
  `Percentage of Population`,
  TotalPopulation
)
#clean comparison data to the columns we need
```


# Visualization
Provide preliminary visualizations in the form of histograms, density plots, scatter
plots, box-plots, and numerical summaries of the data, depending on the type of analysis. What do these visualizations suggest about the hypothesis, model or simulation you are aiming to perform? If you aim to generate further data visualizations, describe them here.

- Diabetes is lower in higher incomes
```{r}

```
- Depression is lower in higher incomes
``` {r, echo=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

depression_plot <- comp_data %>% 
  filter(`Health Status` == "Depression") %>% 
  # make income numeric and make six bins
  mutate(`Income_Bins` = cut(as.numeric(`Income (USD)`), breaks = 6)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = Income_Bins, y = `Percentage of Population`)) + 
  # points added w/ help
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.5, color = "darkorchid", width = 0.2) + 
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.3, outlier.shape = NA) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  # axis labels tilted bc they are long, so they won't overlap
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) + 
  # labeled my axes
  labs( 
    title = "Depression Prevalence across Income Brackets", 
    x = "Income Intervals (USD)", 
    y = "Percentage of Population" 
  )

print(depression_plot)


```

    - the highest income bracket (153-179k/yr) at below 20%
  - We expect a similar result from other mental health illnesses as a generalization due to the illnesses negative effect on the mind       being similar to depression's negative effect.
